Width is the planned difference in this comparison. A difference in tension would introduce a second possible reason for different motion, even though both sounds were recorded by the same microphone.

passage: A bicycle wheel turns freely on a classroom stand. A small patch of bright tape marks one place on its rim. A complete turn means that the patch returns to its starting position after traveling around the wheel. During a short observation, the patch passes the starting position four times. The observer began counting just after releasing it from that position, so the release itself is not a completed turn. The notebook therefore records four complete turns and keeps the starting moment separate from the later returns.

passage: A class is preparing a display about light passing through openings. The display has a cardboard wall, two removable covers, and a lamp aimed at the wall. One cover has a narrow vertical opening; the other has a narrow horizontal opening. Only one cover is used at a time. Place a white sheet behind the wall before turning on the lamp. If the vertical cover is fitted, draw the bright shape on the left side of the record page. If the horizontal cover is fitted, draw it on the right. Write the cover name below each drawing. Keep the lamp and sheet in the same positions when changing covers. This allows visitors to compare the shapes while knowing that the opening changed and the distance between the lamp, wall, and sheet did not.

passage: At a garden observation table, pupils watch a harmless woodlouse move across a divided tray. One half contains damp paper and the other contains dry paper. The tray also has a shaded edge where the animal can leave the open area. The pupils agree to record a choice only when the animal's whole body has crossed the center line. If it pauses with its body across the line, they record an unfinished crossing. During the first observation, its front reaches the damp side while its back remains on the dry side. The recorder leaves the choice column empty and writes unfinished crossing in the notes. This record follows the agreed rule rather than guessing where the animal intended to go. After a brief observation, the pupils return it to the damp place where they found it.

The notebook records which titles people have offered, while the slip records whether a particular copy has been checked. A volunteer finds two copies of the same story, one with a slip and one without. Their matching titles do not allow the volunteer to treat the unchecked copy as though it already carries the other copy's slip.

If a sequence ends before its last required color, do not count that unfinished part as a complete repeat. The first mat has an extra blue strip at one edge after several complete groups. That strip still belongs to the mat, even though it does not complete another blue, blue, yellow group. The comparison therefore distinguishes the number of visible strips from the number of complete repeating groups. Visitors can describe both quantities without pretending that the extra strip has disappeared.

A display note asks visitors to identify a complete repeat before counting how many repeats fit across a mat. If a sequence ends before its last required color, do not count that unfinished part as a complete repeat. The first mat has an extra blue strip at one edge after several complete groups. That strip still belongs to the mat, even though it does not complete another blue, blue, yellow group. The comparison therefore distinguishes the number of visible strips from the number of complete repeating groups. Visitors can describe both quantities without pretending that the extra strip has disappeared.
